The core mathematical structure of this work lies in applying Random Finite Set (RFS) theory to multi-object tracking within sensor networks. It leverages Bayesian inference to estimate object states while accounting for uncertainty in both object count and identities. The framework introduces labeled RFS to associate persistent labels with objects across time, enabling tracking consistency. Key innovations include consensus-based distributed filtering and information fusion techniques such as the normalized weighted geometric mean of Mδ-GLMB and LMB densities. These operations allow for decentralized yet coherent estimation of multiple object trajectories. The theoretical foundation rests upon recursive Bayesian estimation principles extended to handle finite sets of random variables. Dualities emerge between single-object and multi-object filtering approaches, particularly in how consensus protocols propagate beliefs. Failure modes arise from insufficient sensor connectivity, high noise levels, or label collisions during fusion. The derivation hinges on measure-theoretic foundations of RFS, ensuring that all operations remain well-defined even under varying object counts.
